deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a printed page, p. 385, from the Göttingen 'Nachrichten' of the Königliche Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften. Internal evidence dates it to late 1863: Neujahr 1864 is announced as future, and the next page has a paper presented on 6 December. The page is the end of the Society's annual report of prize questions and business, and it was filed in Riemann's bundle 'R.Primzahlen' as Bl. 12. The archival folio number '12' is pencilled in the right margin. The '36' at the foot is the printer's signature (Bogen) mark, not a page number.

Content of the page:
(1) The historical-philological class sets a prize question for November 1865: an accurate history of Damascus from the earliest times to the fall of the Caliphate. It is given in Latin and in German.
(2) Entry rules. Competing essays must reach the Society post-free before the end of September of the year concerned. Each must carry a motto and be accompanied by a sealed slip giving the author's name and residence. The prize for each question is fifty ducats.
(3) The questions of the Wedekind foundation for German history (second administrative period) are said to be republished in Nr. 8 of this year's Nachrichten.
(4) From New Year 1864 the Dieterich'sche Buchhandlung takes over publication of the Nachrichten. They will appear with better presentation and in Latin type.
(5) A report on Gauss's Werke. Volume I was presented complete at last year's session. Volumes II and III are now being printed simultaneously. Volume II, containing a very significant part of the Nachlass, would already have appeared but for unforeseen editorial difficulties (this sentence continues on p. 386).

Why the page is in Riemann's prime-number bundle: almost certainly because of the preceding page, p. 384. There the mathematical class sets the prize question for November 1864 on whether there are infinitely many twin primes (p, p+2). This page is simply the continuation of that printed announcement. It also carries the general entry rules and the prize amount that apply to the twin-prime question.

There are no derivations to reconstruct and no implicit steps to fill in.
errors: No mathematical content, hence no mathematical errors.
Printer's typo in the original: 'Gellschaft' for 'Gesellschaft' in the German version of the Damascus question. The machine transcription reproduces it faithfully.
'funfzig' (for 'fünfzig') is a period spelling, not an error.

results.what: Printed context only: the general prize rules (deadline end of September, motto, sealed name slip, 50 ducats). These apply among others to the 1864 Göttingen prize question on the infinitude of twin primes, printed on the preceding page.
results.modern_name: Twin prime conjecture (context only; not stated on this page)
results.usually_credited_to: Usually traced to de Polignac (1849) as part of his more general conjecture; the 1863/64 Göttingen prize question is a documented public statement of the twin-prime problem.

It contains no mathematics by Riemann. Its presence in the prime-number bundle is explained by the twin-prime prize question on the previous page.
